d.g: Any bird of the subfamily Milvinae, with long wings and weak legs, feeding mostly on carrion and spending long periods soaring; specifically, the red kite (Milvus milvus) and the black kite (Milvus migrans).
A bird of the genus Elanus, having thin pointed wings, that preys on rodents and hunts by hovering; also, any bird of related genera in the subfamily Elaninae.
Some species in the subfamily Perninae.

kite.e: The noun is from Middle English kyte, kīte, kete (“a kite endemic to Europe, especially the red kite (Milvus milvus)”), from Old English cȳta (“kite; bittern”), from Proto-West Germanic *kūtijō, diminutive of Proto-West Germanic *kūt (“bird of prey”), from Proto-Indo-European *gewH-d- (“to cry, screech”). …

d.g: a small shrubby spiny tree cultivated for its maroon-purple fruit with sweet purple pulp tasting like gooseberries;  Sri Lanka and India
An acquaintance or a friend.
A person who is not related to a child but has social connections to the child's family, especially when considered as a caregiver or possible caregiver for the child.

kith.e: From Middle English kitthe (“kinsmen, relations”), from Old English cȳþþ, cȳþþu (“kinship, kinsfolk, relations”), from Proto-Germanic *kunþiþō (“knowledge, acquaintance”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵneh₃- (“to know”). …

d.g: Art, decorative objects, and other forms of representation of questionable artistic or aesthetic value; a representation that is excessively sentimental, overdone, or vulgar.
Of art and decor: of questionable aesthetic value; excessively sentimental, overdone or vulgar.
d.x: […] a picture of lemur-eyed children of the sort one sees in the kitscher sort of Italian restaurant […]

kitsch.e: From German Kitsch, from dialectal kitschen (“to coat, to smear”); the word and concept were popularized in the 1930s by several critics who contrasted it with avant-garde art.

d.g: A piece of partially split bamboo, once used to crush the hand as a form of torture in India.
A young cat, especially before sexual maturity (reached at about seven months).
A young rabbit, rat, hedgehog, squirrel, fox, beaver, badger, etc.
A moth of the genus Furcula.
A term of endearment, especially for a woman.
d.x: Speak only when spoken to, kitten.

kitten.e: From Middle English kitoun, kytton, kyton, keton (“kitten”), of obscure origin. Seemingly from, and usually explained as being from, unattested Anglo-Norman *kitoun, *ketun (compare Old French chitoun, cheton, chaton (“kitten”), diminutive of cat, chat (“cat”)); whence Modern French chaton (“kitten”). …

d.g: Either of two small gulls in the genus Rissa of the family Laridae that nest in colonies on sea cliffs and spend the winter on the open ocean.
the black-legged kittiwake (Rissa tridactyla), no other kittiwake being found in Europe.

kittiwake.e: Originally Scots, imitative of the bird's call.

d.g: A palm of species Caryota urens, native to the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia that yields a sap from which sugar can be made.
A fiber obtained from the leaves of the palm.
A young cat; a kitten.
d.x: He said there was a beast with fangs in the alley, but it turned out to be a cute little kitty.

d.g: An adult cat; also (often childish), sometimes in the form Kitty: a pet name for a cat of any age.
d.x: Here, kitty kitty! Nice kitty!

d.g: Synonym of pussy (“vulva and/or vagina”).
d.x: The way Tariq was licking her kitty had her clutching the sheets.

d.g: Synonym of jack (“a small, typically white, ball used as the target ball in bowls”).

kitty.e: From kitt(en) + -y (diminutive suffix). Compare Dutch katje (“kitty”). Etymology 1 sense 2 (“vulva and/or vagina”) is probably modelled after the use of pussy to refer to the body part, from the appearance of an unshaven vulva.

d.g: The toddy palm Caryota urens.
a lake in the mountains of central Africa between Congo and Rwanda
A flightless bird of the order Apterygiformes native to New Zealand.
Alternative letter-case form of Kiwi (“a person from New Zealand”).
A New Zealand dollar.
A kiwi fruit.

kiwi.e: Māori kiwibor. English kiwi Borrowed from Māori kiwi.

d.g: Alternative spelling of kibitz.
d.x: So how it’s gonna go is we’re gonna talk for about 45 minutes. We’re just gonna kibbitz here; that’s Yiddish for just kinda like […]

d.g: To make small talk or idle chatter.
d.x: Louise and I used to head down to the coffee shop and just sit for hours and kibitz.

d.g: To give unsolicited or unwanted advice or make unhelpful or idle comments, especially to someone playing a game.
d.x: Quit kibitzing! You're giving away my hand!

d.g: To watch a card or board game.
d.x: When it was my turn to stay in the office until 11 pm. closing, I kibitzed on their poker games and heard some colorful tales.

kibitz.e: From Yiddish קיבעצן (kibetsn), cognate to German kiebitzen (“to look on”), from German Kiebitz (“lapwing”), from Middle High German gibiz (“plover”), imitative of its cry. Compare peewit.

d.g: Chiefly in put on the kibosh or put the kibosh on: something which checks or restrains.
d.x: Once or twice triumphant memories of the earlier incidents nerve his face for awhile. "I put the ky-bosh on his little game," he remarks.

d.g: To decisively put a stop to or terminate (someone or something).
d.x: Fortunately the FA [Football Association], in a rare moment of decisiveness, stepped in to kibosh the plan.

kibosh.e: The origin of the noun is uncertain; the following etymologies have been suggested: * According to Gerald Leonard Cohen, Stephen Goranson, and Matthew Little, at present the most likely derivation is as a non-rhotic variant of kurbash (“heavy whip, lash”), from Arabic كُرْبَاج (kurbāj, “lash, whip”), or from its etymon …

d.g: To seize or detain a person unlawfully and move or conceal them; sometimes for ransom.
d.x:
Hello, ladies! How’s the Big Apple?
Rotten, Jerry! Clover's been kidnapped!
Oh, dear! That's the second time this month!

d.g: The crime, or an instance, of kidnapping.

kidnap.e: From kid + nap (“to nab; to grab”). Originally Thieves' cant, referring to the practice of stealing children and shipping them to colonies or plantations as laborers. First attested c. 1680.

d.g: To start (a fire) or light (a torch, a match, coals, etc.).
d.x: If a person kindle a fire in the house of another person, let him pay for the house to the owner, if it be burned.

d.g: To arouse or inspire (a passion, etc).
d.x: He kindled an enthusiasm for the project in his fellow workers.

d.g: To begin to grow or take hold.
d.x: The doctor now interposed, and prevented the effects of a wrath which was kindling between Jones and Thwackum […]

d.g: A group of kittens.
d.x: A kindle of kittens.

kindle.e: From Middle English kyndelen, from Old Norse kynda (“to inflame”), from Proto-Germanic *kundijaną.
